ai_answer: The Supreme Court has held that Article 21 of the Constitution protects the right to life and personal liberty as a fundamental right that is not limited to a single source.  In *Kaushal Kishor v. State of Uttar Pradesh* the Court emphasized that Article 21 is not the sole repository of the right to life and personal liberty, and that the right is broad and evolving.  *Unni Krishnan J.P. v. State of Andhra Pradesh* further clarified that the term ‘personal liberty’ includes privacy, dignity and the freedom to move, and that these attributes are inseparable from the right to life.  In *People’s Union for Civil Liberties v. Union of India* the Court reiterated that personal liberty is of the widest amplitude and that unenumerated rights such as the right to privacy, the right to go abroad and the right against solitary confinement fall within Article 21.  Together, these decisions establish that Article 21 guarantees a comprehensive protection of life and personal liberty, encompassing privacy, dignity, freedom of movement and other related liberties.

question: freedom of speech and reasonable restrictions under Article 19

SHREYA SINGHAL versus UNION OF INDIA

ai_answer: The Supreme Court has held that Article 19(1)(a) does not confer an absolute right to freedom of speech and expression; it is subject to reasonable restrictions enumerated in Article 19(2).  The Court has repeatedly emphasized that the right is accompanied by duties towards fellow citizens and society, and that any speech which does not conform to the content of Article 19(1)(a) may be restrained.  Accordingly, the State may impose restrictions on speech that is hateful, defamatory, or otherwise contrary to the interests of the community, provided such restrictions are made only on the grounds listed in Article 19(2) and are reasonable in the circumstances.
